text: Operational facilities and control systems have very different requirements from the cutting-edge of technology, though, with a need for reliability and quantifi- ability. This differs greatly from usage for language processing and image processing, where a larger degree of error is generally acceptable. Identifying areas within operations that would benefit directly from the current state of AI/ML research is a challenge outside of needs that mimic those in industry (e.g. image and language processing). Many of the needs fall under reliability and control theory, with theories that have been generally well-developed for decades. Similar to the issues discussed above, such techniques are relatively rare in operations due to the conservative nature of such organizations, limitedR&Dbudgets, andtheriskofdamagetoequipment. Theequipmentusedforcontrols has also led to a number of limitations or workarounds being necessary. This is particularly true with PLCs (Programmable Logic Controllers) and proprietary vendor-provided hardware. The widespread use of such equipment leads to only a few opportunities for machine learning wrapped around them — optimization techniques, slow control, and protocol and failure analysis. PLCs in particular are still using proprietary tooling and communication architectures. One important point was consistent across every interview: generally, no one knows who owns the data or models created within the community. This problem leads to other negative consequences, in particular for risk-adverse organizations. This confusion regarding IP ownership is independent of funding rules or organization size. A significant advantage of the accelerator community, which was brought up in several interviews, is that scientific collaborations often enjoy a feeling of openness, regardless of internal policies or specific regulations on IP. Individuals in the community often benefit from this advantage, in spite of organizational challenges and bureaucratic processes. Industry,academiaandgovernmentareconvergingontheuseof pytorch[16]astheirAI/MLframework of choice. This is in part due to challenges inherent in using TensorFlow [21], due to Google leading the project. The pytorch framework and organization is growing rapidly, and its ease of use has been noted by many organizations. ML for operational control is still not mainstream for operations in US facilities, with facilities only recently implementing test projects for portions of their ML needs (e.g. deployment techniques, data analy- sis). Most of these prototype projects are focused on optimization techniques, looking at ways to minimize systemdowntimeorassistwithmachinealignmentandstart-up. Oneofthemostpopulartoolsinuseacross multiple facilities, internationally, is the SLAC-developed xopt/badger toolkit [10, 11]. AI/ML is very different from other technologies as to where cutting-edge research is occurring. Much of the most advanced research has come out of large companies, such as Tesco, Microsoft, or Google, and not out of research institutions. This leads to important differences in how collaborations should be structured, as is discussed below.
